job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

response.passage: Dear Diary, today our science teacher explained how satellites are the silent heroes of our modern world. I was surprised to learn that satellites do not need engines running constantly to stay in orbit; they simply move at high speeds, falling around the Earth due to gravity. I used to think they were like airplanes that need fuel to keep moving, but they actually coast in a vacuum. We discussed geostationary satellites, which orbit at about 36,000 km, much higher than the International Space Station. Because they match Earth's rotation, they appear fixed above one spot, allowing our DTH television to work without us constantly adjusting our dishes. I also learned that GPS does not track my phone; instead, my phone receives signals from at least four satellites to calculate its own position. It is fascinating how remote sensing satellites use special sensors to detect crop health by measuring light beyond what our eyes see, proving they do much more than just take simple photographs. Even in the dark, these satellites use radar to monitor cyclones, so they never stop working. It is amazing how these machines, launched by powerful rockets that push against their own exhaust rather than air, keep us connected and safe every single day.
response.summary: Satellites orbit Earth using gravity and high speeds rather than constant engine power. They provide essential services like global positioning, weather monitoring, and communication by staying in specific orbits or using advanced sensors.
